questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.learningObjective: Correct the stated energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.stem: A student wrote that the first industrial revolution was powered by electric power from the start. Which correction should be made to that mistake?

options.text: Replace it with coal and steam, which supplied the energy for early industrial machinery
options.misconception: keeps the modern power source and only rewrites the dates

options.text: Replace it with water power alone, since coal was not used in industry before the nineteenth century
options.misconception: assumes coal was unused in industry before 1800

options.text: Replace it with wind power, because windmills drove the first factories
options.misconception: confuses traditional windmills with powered factories

options.text: Replace it with coal, since coal and steam, not electricity, powered early industrial machinery

questions.explanation: The correction is that early industrial machinery was driven by coal and steam, with water and wind minor. Electric power belongs to a later phase, so redating the mistake would not fix it.
questions.hint: Ask what actually turned the early machines.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the factory system did to labour
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what the factory system did to labour

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: a pupil's summary said that the factory system gave workers shorter hours and more rest than they had before, because the employer needed them fresh for the machines. The teacher wrote in the margin that the summary had confused the employer's wish with the hours actually kept, and asked for the effect that the system did have.

questions.stem: Judging from the worksheet note above, what correction should the pupil make about labour?

options.text: That factory workers also gained literacy and independence, so the system improved workers' lives
options.misconception: invents an educational gain the note does not describe

options.text: That the factory system replaced family work entirely, leaving no household production at all
options.misconception: overstates the disappearance of household work

options.text: That the factory system brought workers under strict time discipline and supervision at the workplace
That hours in factories were always shorter than in domestic work for the same trade
options.misconception: keeps the pupil's claim with only the word always changed

questions.explanation: The factory system put work under clocking, supervision and strict discipline, and the note says the pupil confused employer preference with hours kept. Educational gains are not described.
questions.hint: Ask what the employer actually required day by day.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rulebook that measured work
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a rulebook of rates and times was for
questions.stem: I found a workbook that said the early factory rulebook simply recorded how many hours each worker had put in. Explain what such rulebooks were really for and how they were used.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that the rulebooks were a system of measurement and payment: each operation was given a standard rate and a standard time, the output of each worker was counted, and wages were calculated from that count rather than from the hours spent. It would add that the rules let managers compare workers, set prices, plan output and discipline labour, and that they also created disputes, since a count that favoured the employer could be challenged by the workers it measured.

questions.explanation: The item tests the real purpose of the rulebook, which was measurement for payment and management, not hours recording. Treating it as a payroll convenience, or ignoring its disputes, is incomplete.
questions.hint: Ask what the numbers were used to work out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a railway joined together
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a railway joined together
questions.stem: A visitor told me a railway had simply shortened the journey between two towns. Which correction should I make to that mistake?

options.text: A railway always reduced travel because journeys became cheaper than walking
options.misconception: asserts a cost claim the mistake did not make

options.text: A railway was only a faster version of the old cart road and changed nothing else
options.misconception: treats the railway as a pure change of speed

options.text: A railway mainly served the army and had almost no effect on ordinary trade
options.misconception: assigns the railway a narrow military purpose only

options.text: A railway joined many towns into one connected market for goods, labour and news

questions.explanation: The correction is that a railway did far more than shorten journeys: it tied scattered towns into one market, moving goods, workers, mail and news along a network. Speed alone is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the line connected, not how fast it ran.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mill moved to the railway
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken explanation of why a mill moved to the railway

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: a pupil wrote that a mill moved to the railway simply because the railway was an exciting new thing and the mill's owner liked it. The teacher replied that the move was made for cost reasons, that the mill had stood where water power was available, and that water power was not always enough to run the mill through a busy season.

questions.stem: Using the worksheet note above, what correction should the pupil make about the mill?

options.text: The mill moved because the new site had more workers living nearby than the old one
options.misconception: gives a labour explanation the note does not mention

options.text: The mill moved because the owner wanted a larger building for the family to live in
options.misconception: invents a family motive the note never records

options.text: The mill moved because the railway company offered to buy the mill at a high price
options.misconception: asserts a purchase motive the note does not contain

options.text: The mill moved to cut costs and add power beyond what the old water supply could give

questions.explanation: The teacher attributes the move to cost and to power supply, since the old site depended on water that failed in busy seasons. Novelty and a high purchase price are absent from the note.
questions.hint: Ask what the mill lacked at the old site.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The housing that urbanisation produced
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of the housing produced by urbanisation
questions.stem: Someone told me that industrialisation simply put everyone into new houses straight away. Which correction should be made to that mistake?

options.text: Urbanisation built houses faster than people could arrive, so empty streets appeared first
options.misconception: reverses the order of building and arrival

options.text: Housing was never a problem, because families moved out before the new houses were finished
options.misconception: claims the housing shortage never existed at all

options.text: Housing was built quickly and cheaply, so workers crowded into dense, poorly built districts
Housing was provided by employers in good condition, so overcrowding was rare
options.misconception: assumes employers built fine housing in bulk

questions.explanation: Housing was rushed and cheap, and workers crowded into dense districts with poor sanitation, which is why conditions became a scandal. Fine employer housing contradicts the record.
questions.hint: Ask what the standard of the new housing was.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A surveyor's account of dwellings
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a surveyor's return recorded

stimulus.body: Survey note: the surveyor's return for the district records the condition of the houses rather than the wealth of the families. It notes one cellar room kept for two families, an outside privy shared by twelve households, and a street where the houses were built so close together that no daylight reached the back rooms. In another street it notes three houses with glass windows and an area kept clear in front.

questions.stem: Using the surveyor's return above, what does the account actually record?

options.text: The incomes of the families, ranked from the richest households to the poorest
options.misconception: reads a condition survey as an income survey

options.text: The physical state of dwellings, including crowding, light and shared facilities
The political opinions of the residents, noted by the surveyor during his visits
options.misconception: invents a political record the note never mentions

options.text: The exact population of each street, counted as the surveyor walked through it
options.misconception: substitutes a headcount for what the return actually records

questions.explanation: The return records observable conditions of the housing itself, such as shared privies, dark back rooms and overcrowding, not money or opinion. Income rankings and headcounts are not it.
questions.hint: Ask what the surveyor could see on his rounds.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A public health measure and its effect
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a public health measure achieved
questions.stem: I read a claim that a clean water measure had ended the sickness in the district. Explain what such a measure did and what it did not do.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that providing a clean water supply and building sewers removed the contaminated water that had been carrying the disease, so cases fell sharply in the areas served. It would add that the measure did not touch overcrowding, damp courtyards, cellar dwellings or the pile of rubbish in the streets, and that other causes of illness continued, so the fall in deaths should be credited to the water and sewer work rather than to the measure solving every problem of industrial housing.

questions.explanation: The item tests the limits of a single public health measure as well as its effect. Crediting it with curing every problem of industrial housing misstates the case.
questions.hint: Ask what the measure left untouched.

questions.topic: The energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.learningObjective: Correct the stated energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.stem: A colleague said the first industrial revolution was powered by steam alone, from the very beginning. Which correction covers the whole error?

options.text: Steam was invented at the start, and coal was only discovered when the pits filled with water
options.misconception: reverses the order of steam and coal in the story

options.text: Steam was never used in industry, and everything was powered by hand and wind
options.misconception: denies industrial steam altogether

options.text: Coal was used first, and steam arrived only after every factory had closed
options.misconception: invents a closure of factories the record does not show

options.text: Coal and steam together powered the early machinery, with electricity belonging to a later phase

questions.explanation: The correction is that early industry drew on coal and steam, with electricity arriving in a later phase, so the error is about the energy base and its timing. The alternatives reverse the order.
questions.hint: Ask which energy source the early machines used.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the factory system did to labour
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what the factory system did to labour

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: a pupil wrote that before the factories there had been no work at all for the poor, since everyone had been idle until the mills opened. The teacher corrected this, saying that cottage industries and seasonal work had existed for centuries, and that what changed was where and how the work was organised.

questions.stem: On the evidence of the worksheet note above, what correction is needed about labour?

options.text: That there had been plenty of work before, so the factory system added nothing to it
options.misconception: ignores the change the teacher described

options.text: That there had been no work, but it had all been done in fields rather than in homes
options.misconception: shifts the error from work to its location

options.text: That work existed but was scattered, seasonal and organised in homes rather than in one workplace
That the factory system ended the practice of women working at home on spinning wheels
options.misconception: claims a practice ended that the note does not mention

questions.explanation: Work long existed in scattered, seasonal household production, and the factory system reorganised where and how it was done rather than inventing work. Doing nothing misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask what the teacher said had changed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rulebook that measured work
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a rulebook of rates and times was for
questions.stem: A school inspector asked why early factory owners needed written rules for every job. Which statement corrects the mistake that the rules were simply to keep workers in line?

options.text: The rules were mainly to record each worker's name and address for the tax office
options.misconception: assigns the rulebook a fiscal purpose it did not have

options.text: The rules set output rates and piece rates, so pay and prices could be calculated from work done
The rules existed to allow workers to set their own pace and hours each week
options.misconception: reverses the purpose of the rules they describe

options.text: The rules were drawn up by the workers themselves to settle disputes fairly
options.misconception: gives the rulebook to the wrong side of the relationship

questions.explanation: The rulebook defined standard rates and times so output could be counted and wages and prices calculated from it. It was not a name register, and employers wrote it.
questions.hint: Ask what the numbers in it were for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a railway joined together
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a railway joined together

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: I corrected a pupil who wrote that the railway line was built to carry coal to the local market. The note in my copy says coal traffic was a small part of the early traffic and that the main cargoes were raw materials and finished goods moving between towns that had never been closely linked before, along with milk and letters for the villages on the line.

questions.stem: The entry I corrected in the copy shows that the railway carried what?

options.text: It carried military stores, and civilian traffic was kept off the line
options.misconception: invents a military restriction the note does not mention

options.text: It carried coal alone, because the line existed to move coal from the pits
options.misconception: keeps the pupil's claim that coal was the main cargo

options.text: It carried only passengers, since freight was moved by road until the goods lines opened
options.misconception: ignores the freight the note records

options.text: It carried a general traffic of goods, mail and farm produce between newly linked places

questions.explanation: The note describes general freight, mail and farm produce moving between places newly linked by the line, with coal only a small part. Coal alone contradicts it.
questions.hint: Ask what the line moved for the towns on it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mill moved to the railway
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken explanation of why a mill moved to the railway
questions.stem: I was asked why mills were willing to leave good riverside sites to build beside a railway. Explain why the usual reasons for such a move were power and cost rather than proximity to buyers.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that a mill site was chosen first for the power available, and that a mill standing on a river was limited by the flow of water, which could run out in a dry season or at peak demand, so output was irregular and costly to expand. Moving to a site beside a railway, where steam could be used, gave a firm and enlargable power supply and cut the cost of moving bulky inputs and finished goods, while the buyers stayed where they had always been and were reached by the same line.

questions.explanation: The item tests the real logic of mill siting: reliable power and cheaper transport of heavy inputs, not proximity to buyers. Answers resting on fashion or custom miss the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the river could not promise.

questions.topic: The housing that urbanisation produced
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of the housing produced by urbanisation
questions.stem: Someone told me that industrial towns were full of neat houses because the new workers insisted on good conditions. Which correction should I make?

options.misconception: invents a planning rule the case never records

options.text: The houses were neat because employers wanted their workers contented and healthy
options.misconception: assumes employers built fine housing from kindness

options.text: The houses were crowded and cheaply built, since housing had to be provided quickly for crowds of workers
The houses were neat because building standards were already high in the countryside
options.misconception: moves the improvement into the countryside without evidence

questions.explanation: Housing was built quickly and cheaply to house crowds of workers, so districts were crowded, badly lit and poorly drained. A planning rule and employer kindness are not recorded.
questions.hint: Ask why the building had to be so quick.

questions.topic: A surveyor's account of dwellings
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a surveyor's return recorded

stimulus.body: Survey note: the return for the quarter was asked for in a form that asked only about houses: the number of rooms, whether they were underground, whether the street was paved and drained, where the water came from and where the sewage went. The surveyor added in his own line that he had been asked not to record the wages of the families.

questions.stem: The form for the quarterly return asked for what?

options.text: The wages of each household, so that the district's wealth could be measured
options.misconception: ignores the instruction to leave wages unrecorded

options.text: Details of the houses, such as rooms, light, drainage, water and sewage arrangements
The number of children in each house, as a sign of the district's health
options.misconception: substitutes a household count for a housing return

options.text: The occupations of household heads, so that the factory could plan its labour
options.misconception: invented a factory labour survey the note never records

questions.explanation: The form asked about rooms, light, paving, water and sewage, so the survey recorded housing conditions and services, with wages excluded. Ranking wealth and counting children are different aims.
questions.hint: Read the list of things the form asks.

questions.stem: A pamphlet claimed that a sewer built under the town had removed every cause of disease in the district. Which correction should be made to that mistake?

options.text: The sewers raised the death rate, because they carried the waste to the nearby river
options.misconception: reverses the recorded effect of the measure

options.text: The sewers had no effect on disease, since the real cause was the crowded housing
options.misconception: denies the measured effect on waterborne illness

options.misconception: invents a seasonal pattern the case never gives

options.text: The sewers cut disease from contaminated water but left crowding, damp and rubbish untouched

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.learningObjective: Correct the stated energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.stem: A claim I read held that the early factories ran on electricity because the machines needed steady power. Explain what actually powered the early industrial machinery and why the difference mattered.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that the early machinery was driven by coal burned to make steam, with water wheels providing a useful supplement in some places. It would add that the difference mattered because steam gave a power supply that did not depend on a river, so output could be regular, extended and concentrated in a mill town, whereas water power tied a factory to a particular site and a variable flow, and electricity was only introduced later, changing the location and scale of production again.

questions.explanation: The item tests the energy base of early industry and the consequences that followed from it. Answers that name a modern source, or that name coal without explaining why it mattered, are incomplete.
questions.hint: Ask what a factory on a river could not control.

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: a pupil wrote that the factory system gave children more leisure because machines did the heavy work. questions.stem: The correction in my copy describes children in factories in which way?

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change the teacher describes

options.text: They were barred from factory work and kept entirely at home
options.misconception: claims a total exclusion the note contradicts

options.text: They worked long, supervised hours, with discipline enforced by bells and foremen
They worked only when they wanted to, and could leave whenever they pleased
options.misconception: describes a freedom the note says the system removed

questions.explanation: The teacher's comment describes long hours for small pay under bell-ruled discipline watched by foremen, so the claim of more leisure must be reversed. Personal freedom is excluded too.
questions.hint: Ask who controlled the pace of the day.

options.misconception: adds a closure effect the note never describes

questions.explanation: The returns show a wide traffic between places that had been separate markets, so the railway created one connected market and moved prices with it. Coal alone is contradicted.

questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a surveyor's return recorded
questions.stem: I read a surveyor's return that recorded only the state of the houses. Explain why a survey of this kind was carried out and what its findings were used for.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the survey was carried out to establish the actual state of workers' housing after complaint, so that the conditions could be documented rather than argued about. It would note that the returns recorded overcrowding, cellar rooms, shared privies, unlit courts and unpaved streets, and that these findings were used to justify building authorities, new water supplies, sewers and minimum standards, which in turn made the survey a tool for reform rather than a simple record.

questions.explanation: The item tests the purpose and the use of such a survey. Answers that treat it as a routine census, or that omit its use in pressing for reform, miss the point of the return.
questions.hint: Ask what the recorded facts were used to justify.

options.misconception: invents a closure and reverses the order

options.misconception: redates coal instead of correcting the power source

options.text: Keep coal but identify it as fuel for steam, with water and electricity in their proper places

questions.explanation: The teacher says the coal that mattered fed boilers raising steam, with water wheels still turning some machines and electricity arriving later. The alternatives replace the fuel wrongly.

questions.stem: I was asked how a rulebook of rates and times could be used against the workers who measured themselves. Explain how the measurement system could be turned to the employer's advantage.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the system turned on the standard time allowed for each piece, and that once the output was counted the employer could set the rate for the job, compare a worker's count with a colleague's, and dock the difference when a count was short, or replace a slow hand with a quick one. questions.explanation: The correction says bells, checked gates and foremen's records took the working day out of the worker's hands. A voluntary choice and restored household control are contrary to it.
questions.hint: Ask who now decided the hours.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rulebook that measured work
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a rulebook of rates and times was for
questions.stem: An inspector asked why the rulebook listed a standard time for each job as well as a standard rate. Which statement answers best?

options.text: Because the times were kept so that the employers could find out who arrived early
options.misconception: confuses standard times with attendance records

options.text: Because wages and prices were calculated from the counted output against those standards
Because the times allowed the government to check that the working day was legal
options.misconception: invents an official inspection of the rulebook

options.text: Because the times were needed to train new workers who had never done the job
options.misconception: makes the standards a training device, not a measuring one

questions.explanation: Standards for time and rate let output be counted against a fixed norm, so wages, prices and comparisons all follow from the same figures. Attendance and training are different purposes.
questions.hint: Ask what the counted output was compared with.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a railway joined together
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a railway joined together

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: the entry I corrected said the railway's chief purpose was to bring coal cheaply to the inland markets. The returns in my copy show coal as a modest share of the first year's traffic, while cotton cloth, iron goods, grain, timber, live cattle and mail made up most of it, with the traffic running between towns whose markets had previously been separate and whose prices had differed from one week to the next.

questions.stem: The returns I corrected mention coal only as what?

options.text: A modest share of a wide traffic that merged markets which had been separate
The whole traffic, because coal was the line's true and only purpose
options.misconception: keeps the pupil's coal-only claim for the traffic

options.text: Nothing at all, since freight was left to the roads for the first decade
options.misconception: ignores the goods the returns list

options.text: A harmful share, because the pits flooded the local markets with cheap coal
options.misconception: invents a flooding effect the note never records

questions.explanation: The returns list a broad traffic and show markets merging, so the line's effect was far wider than moving coal. Coal only, freight left to the roads and a harmful share are all unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask what the returns list and what prices did.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mill moved to the railway
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken explanation of why a mill moved to the railway
questions.stem: I was asked to explain why a mill might not move to a railway even when a line passed close by. Explain what could keep it where it was.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that a mill had reasons to stay, among them the cost of moving heavy machinery and rebuilding a working building, the value of the water rights it already held, the length of its leases and the sunk cost of its yard and outbuildings. It would add that a mill also weighed what it would gain, since steam and a rail connection brought power and cheaper handling but also a dependence on the railway company for power and for access to buyers, so a mill with plenty of water and short contracts might reasonably stay put.

questions.explanation: The item tests the counter-arguments to relocation as well as the reasons for it. Answers that list only the advantages of moving, or that assume every mill moved, miss the reasoning.
questions.hint: Ask what a mill had to lose in moving.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The housing that urbanisation produced
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of the housing produced by urbanisation
questions.stem: I was asked to judge the claim that the housing of the industrial towns was worse than the cottages people had left. Which statement is the fairest assessment?

options.text: It was much worse, since workers were packed into rooms that had once held a family
options.misconception: accepts the claim without weighing the old conditions

options.text: It was much better, since every family had a kitchen and a washhouse in the new dwellings
options.misconception: invents amenities the new housing often lacked

options.text: It was different rather than simply worse, trading light and space for income close to the works
It was identical, since the new houses were built on the same plan as the old cottages
options.misconception: claims identical housing plans without evidence

questions.explanation: The fairest assessment weighs both sides: the new dwellings were darker and more crowded than cottages, but wages were near the works and income steadier. Simply worse or better oversimplifies.
questions.hint: Ask what the new housing gained as well as lost.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A surveyor's account of dwellings
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a surveyor's return recorded

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: the pupil said the surveyor's return was a list of the district's rich and poor households. My correction points out that the return asked about rooms, cellars, courtyards, privies, lighting, drainage and water, that the surveyor marked the condition of each street on the plan, and that the form carried no column for money at all.

questions.stem: The return I read has no money column, so what does the survey record?

options.text: A ranking of households by rent, with the poorest listed first
options.misconception: invents a rent ranking the form never carried

options.text: The state of the houses and the services around them, not household wealth
The inhabitants of each street so that the plan could be redrawn
options.misconception: substitutes a headcount for a condition survey

options.text: The occupations of household heads for the factory's records
options.misconception: supplies an occupation column the form did not have

questions.explanation: The form asked about rooms, privies, lighting, drainage and water and carried no money column, so it recorded the condition of property. A rent ranking and an occupation list are absent.
questions.hint: Notice what the form deliberately left out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A public health measure and its effect
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a public health measure achieved
questions.stem: A reader asked how a single measure of clean water could change the health of a whole district. Which statement explains it correctly?

options.text: It removed the fouled water that carried the disease, so cases fell where it reached
It strengthened the bodies of the residents, so they fought the sickness better
options.misconception: invites a physiological effect the measure did not have

options.text: It drew the damp out of the ground under the houses, curing the damp itself
options.misconception: confuses a water supply with a drainage scheme

options.text: It made the district more temperate, and warmth was the true cause of illness
options.misconception: invents a climate effect the record does not support

questions.explanation: Clean water removed the fouled supply that carried disease, so cases fell sharply where the scheme reached. A drying of the ground and a warmer climate are not effects it had.
questions.hint: Ask what exactly the water was carrying.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.learningObjective: Correct the stated energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.stem: At the seminar I was asked to explain why the energy base of the first industrial revolution is the wrong place to start for later developments. Explain what the early energy base made possible and what it ruled out.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that coal and steam gave the early factories a power supply they could place anywhere with coal and transport, so production could be concentrated, enlarged and run for long hours rather than following the flow of a river, and it made the concentrated factory town possible. It would add that this still tethered industry to coal prices and to the smoke and railways the coal required, and that it was these constraints, rather than any lack of invention, that electricity and later power sources were brought in to remove.

questions.explanation: The item tests both what the early energy base enabled and what it could not overcome. Answers that only praise coal and steam, or only list their drawbacks, miss the argument about what came next.
questions.hint: Ask what the coal itself made necessary.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the factory system did to labour
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what the factory system did to labour

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: the correction I wrote notes that the household system had already put women and children to work in spinning and weaving for the market long before the factories, and that the change was not from idleness to work but from work scattered through households to work gathered under one roof and one clock. It adds that the new system drew the whole family into a longer and stricter working day.

questions.stem: The correction I wrote notes the household work to have been what?

options.text: Work that ended once the factories opened, because home spinning was made illegal
options.misconception: promises an end the note does not report

options.text: Work that gave women more control over their own hours than the factory did
options.misconception: invents a control the note says was tightened

options.text: Work that already existed, so the change was where and how the day was controlled
Work that was shorter than factory hours, so the change was an increase in rest
options.misconception: reverses the note's statement about a longer day

questions.explanation: The note says work was already done in households and that the change was where it happened and who controlled the clock. Ending child labour and a shorter day are excluded.
questions.hint: Ask what the note says the clock changed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rulebook that measured work
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a rulebook of rates and times was for
questions.stem: Another colleague said the rulebook of rates and times was merely a way of counting hours. Which statement gives the best correction?

options.text: It was unnecessary bureaucracy, added by managers who disliked paying by results
options.misconception: asserts a managerial motive without evidence

options.text: It was a measurement system that turned work into countable units and fixed pay from the count
It was a legal document that bound employers and workers in the same way as a statute
options.misconception: treats a shop rulebook as a legal instrument

options.text: It was a training aid, listing the steps of each job so that new hands could learn them
options.misconception: reassigns the rulebook to training rather than measurement

questions.explanation: The rulebook defined measurable units, allowed output to be counted and fixed pay from that count. Bureaucracy, a statute and a training aid all misidentify its function.
questions.hint: Ask what the count was used to decide.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a railway joined together
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mistaken account of what a railway joined together

stimulus.body: Worksheet note: the pupil's summary described the railway as a faster road between two towns and treated its only importance as saving travel time. My correction records the wider entries: that new towns grew up at the junctions, that prices in the old markets began to follow the prices at the far end of the line, that coal pits opened where the lines reached, and that goods once carried by packhorse were moving in wagonloads.

questions.stem: The summary I corrected describes more than what, and which correction applies?

options.text: It reorganised the economy around a network, moving prices, people and goods between new centres
It mattered only for the two towns it joined, and nothing else in the district changed
options.misconception: keeps the pupil's narrow claim about its reach

options.text: It lowered the price of coal everywhere, because the pits could now supply any district
options.misconception: invents a price effect the note does not record

options.text: It removed the need for packhorse traffic, which is why wagonloads became the only freight
options.misconception: overstates the note's point about wagonloads

questions.explanation: The correction records junctions, converging prices, new coal districts and wagonload freight, which is the economy reorganising around a network. Two towns only goes beyond it.
questions.hint: Ask what grew up where the lines met.
